title: How Family Crests Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain family crests and coats of arms (heraldry): the difference between the terms, their medieval origins on the battlefield, spread to knights, clergy, commoners and surnames, and the role of jousting heralds. They cover the College of Arms in the UK (chartered 1484) and the American College of Heraldry, cadency marks for younger sons, inheritance through male line and rules for women (lozenge, sinister/dexter placement in marriage), Kate Middleton's newly designed arms, the standard elements of a coat of arms (shield, field, supporters, helmet, crest, motto, compartment), heraldic color rules, blazoning language with examples including Ronald Reagan's arms, Scottish clan and tartan registration via the Lord Lyon King of Arms, Scandinavian and Japanese crests (mon), and warnings about paid online crest services. The episode ends with listener mail and promotional plugs.
topics: state seals vs coats of arms

segments.title: Opening banter and family crest setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about Chuck's cold and vitamin C, then introduce family crests and warn that online crest services selling generic crests are likely scams.

segments.title: Family crest vs coat of arms
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difference between a family crest and a coat of arms, offering three explanations (tunic over armor, crest as the top part, crest belonging to a family versus an individual) and noting they are used interchangeably today.
topics: crest vs coat of arms difference

segments.title: Medieval origins and spread of crests
segments.summary: Crests began in the mid-twelfth century to tell knights apart on the battlefield, then spread to pages, squires, priests, commoners and peasants in the thirteenth century, who took surnames from feudal lords. Jousting and tournaments made heralds announce knights by their crests.

segments.title: Heraldry and the College of Arms
segments.summary: Heraldry is the umbrella term. Heralds formed a corporation chartered by Richard the Third in 1484 as the College of Arms, which still registers arms and traces lineage. The American College of Heraldry was founded in 1972 and registers new arms only.

segments.title: Inheritance, cadency and rules for women
segments.summary: Arms pass from father to son, with younger sons adding marks of cadency such as the annulet (ring) and mullet. Daughters can inherit in certain cases, with the shield changed to a lozenge, and marriage combines arms with the wife's placed sinister and the husband's dexter.

segments.title: Kate Middleton's coat of arms
segments.summary: Kate Middleton received a new coat of arms designed by Thomas Woodcock after passing an eminence test. Elements include three acorns for the children, a gold chevron for mountains and her mother's Goldsmith name, a blue ribbon for unmarried status, and red and white colors. Discussion turns to how her arms would combine with the House of Windsor's.

segments.title: Standard elements of a coat of arms
segments.summary: The hosts describe the typical components: shield with field, supporters (figures holding up the shield, described as rampant or passant), helm, mantling, wreath (torse), crest, cornet, motto on a scroll, and compartment. Scottish belts signal clan membership.

segments.title: Heraldic rules, blazoning and the family crest examples
segments.summary: Rules forbid color on color and metal on metal. Chuck and Josh compare their family crests (Chuck's goose-filled arms, Josh's helmet and flag) and mention registries in various countries. Blazoning is the specialized language used to describe arms so artists can draw them, illustrated with the party per pale tree example and Ronald Reagan's arms.

segments.title: Origins by region, state seals, Scotland and Japan
segments.summary: Heraldry likely began in western Europe, especially England, possibly from Scandinavia. US state seals differ from heraldic coats of arms. Scotland requires lineage to claim a tartan or arms under the Lord Lyon King of Arms. Japan has around ten thousand family crests (mon), originally for samurai and now widely used.
topics: state seals vs coats of arms

segments.title: Finding and registering your family crest
segments.summary: Americans can register a new crest with the American College of Heraldry, which requires naming an heir. Brits and others should check official government registries. Josh and Chuck caution against paid online services and note that family pride in crests seems to be declining.

segments.title: Listener mail: Viking ancestry and crest-naming contest
segments.summary: Chuck mentions his dad tracing the family to the Vikings. The hosts read listener submissions to a Facebook movie-title game about a one-room schoolhouse rebuild.

segments.title: Plugs and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts promote the Super Stuff Guide to Happiness and Economics audiobooks, radio station airings, social accounts, email, and the Stuff from the Future video podcast.
